lessons.title: Own Everything, Blame No One
lessons.key_idea: After a deadly friendly fire incident in Ramadi, Jocko took full responsibility instead of blaming others, showing that leaders must own every failure in their world.

lessons.title: No Bad Teams, Only Bad Leaders
lessons.key_idea: In SEAL training, swapping the leaders of the best and worst boat crews flipped the results, proving that leadership determines a team's performance.

lessons.title: Cover and Move
lessons.key_idea: Teams and departments win only when they support each other toward the shared mission rather than competing or working in isolation.

lessons.title: Keep It Simple
lessons.key_idea: Plans and orders must be simple enough that everyone understands them, because complexity collapses under pressure.

lessons.title: Prioritize and Execute
lessons.key_idea: When overwhelmed, a leader should stay calm, pick the single highest priority, focus the team on it, and then move to the next.

lessons.title: Decentralized Command
lessons.key_idea: Leaders should explain the intent behind the mission so that small teams and frontline leaders can make good decisions on their own.

lessons.title: Discipline Equals Freedom
lessons.key_idea: Ownership and the Laws of Combat work only with daily discipline and balance, because a disciplined leader gains more freedom to adapt and lead well.

plan.title: Extreme Ownership
plan.author: Jocko Willink and Leif Babin
plan.confidence_note: I know this book's structure, its core principles, and its main combat and business examples well, though not every passage word for word.
plan.one_liner: Two Navy SEAL officers reveal why great leaders blame no one and own everything.
plan.summary: Jocko Willink and Leif Babin led SEAL Task Unit Bruiser through the brutal Battle of Ramadi in Iraq. After returning home, they began teaching the same leadership lessons to companies. Each chapter pairs a combat story with a business case and a principle you can apply. The core message is simple and demanding. Leaders own everything in their world, including the failures of the people they lead. From there, the authors lay out what they call the Laws of Combat. Teams must support each other, keep plans simple, tackle one priority at a time, and push decisions down to frontline leaders. The book closes by showing that discipline creates freedom, and that good leadership means balancing opposing forces. It is a practical, no-excuses guide for anyone responsible for a team's results.
